meaning: Twilight of the gods (from ragna + rǫk)

phonemes.desc: Initial sound of Ragnarǫk, as attested in the norse tradition.
Subsequent syllables preserve the name's inherited shape.

pronunciation.note: Ragnarǫk is Tier 2 because its Unicode restoration preserves the orthographic signature appropriate to the norse tradition.

domains.title: Doom of the Gods
domains.subtitle: The domain of Ragnarǫk
domains.lead: In the norse tradition, Ragnarǫk governed doom of the gods. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.title: Primary Sphere
cards.body: Ragnarǫk is principally associated with doom of the gods.

cards.title: Cultural Role
cards.body: Worshippers approached Ragnarǫk through cult, myth, and the material culture of the norse world.

symbols.name: Cult site
symbols.meaning: Sanctuary or holy place where Ragnarǫk was honoured

symbols.name: Ritual object
symbols.meaning: Material focus of devotion for Ragnarǫk

mythology.lead: The myths of Ragnarǫk preserve the name's power and personality across generations of retelling.

myths.title: The story of Ragnarǫk
myths.text: Ragnarǫk appears in norse tradition as a figure whose domain over doom of the gods shapes both cosmic order and human experience. The surviving narratives emphasize Ragnarǫk's role, attributes, and relationships with other powers.

lore.syncretism: Norse tradition absorbed and reworked Germanic, Celtic, and Christian influences; medieval Icelandic compilers preserved the myths while Christian frameworks shaped their presentation.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name lives on in modern fantasy, Neopagan practice, Scandinavian heritage, and the global reception of Viking-Age literature. Restoring Ragnarǫk in Unicode preserves the name's cultural specificity against the flattening force of plain ASCII.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Ragnarǫk carries within it a norse understanding of twilight of the gods (from ragna + rǫk). Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form.
sources: The Poetic Edda; The Prose Edda of Snorri Sturluson.
Beekes, R. S. P. Etymological Dictionary of Greek. Leiden: Brill, 2010.
Archaeological evidence includes runestones, grave goods, place-name distributions, and Viking-Age iconography across Scandinavia and the Norse diaspora.
